candidates.story: Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Flash-Lite TTS voice replication
candidates.reason: The exact-timestamped release exposes a consequential deployment choice between a one-year Google-managed voice profile and a seven-day client-managed key, with separate consent, provenance, migration and pricing controls. Current Google documentation and independent FTC and VoiceEQ context support an original operational analysis without relying on launch benchmarks.
The technical issue may be consequential, but the primary page exposed no verifiable exact event time and was bot-gated outside search excerpts. The freshness gate could not be established safely.
Fresh, but the public evidence did not yet expose enough connector-specific permission, write-action and audit detail to support a distinct long-form deployment analysis.
The product integration is fresh, but no meaningful independent evaluation or broad deployment decision was available to earn long-form coverage.

decision.reason: Google's exact-timestamped Gemini 3.8 TTS release makes replicated voices governable project assets with a mandatory enrolment check and materially different storage lifecycles. The article explains the consent-versus-authority boundary, provider-managed versus client-managed retention, provenance limits, migration changes and the January price change without claiming hands-on testing or independent validation of model quality.

claims.text: Google published the selected launch post at 15:15 UTC on 23 September 2026.
Google labels Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Flash-Lite TTS generally available and exposes voice management under /v1beta/voices.
claims.sourceLocator: S3 22 September 2026 release-note entry; the article states the path fact without inferring a separate endpoint lifecycle status.

claims.text: The documented replication flow requires a 10 to 30 second reference recording plus a separate prescribed consent recording from the same adult speaker.
claims.sourceLocator: S2 Audio and consent requirements; S1 voice-owner matching and consent-verification description.

claims.text: Google's enrolment check does not establish continuing authority, contract scope or a later revocation process for every use of the voice.
claims.sourceLocator: S2 documents creation inputs and voice management but not continuing use authority, contract fields or generated-output recall; the article assigns those operational records to the deployer.

claims.text: With store=true, the documented default, Google stores a reusable voice profile, allows up to 200 project profiles and gives the profile a one-year time to live.
claims.sourceLocator: S2 stateful versus stateless modes and retention table.

claims.text: With store=false, Google documents a client-managed encrypted voicekey value, no persisted server-side profile and a seven-day time to live.
claims.sourceLocator: S2 stateless client-managed voice-key section; Index Us did not test persistence or key behaviour.

claims.text: The API documents list, get and delete operations for stored voice profiles but does not say deletion recalls audio already generated from a profile.
claims.sourceLocator: S2 Manage stored replicated voices and complete guide at retrieval; absence is stated as a documentation limit.

claims.text: Availability is route-specific: the launch lists Gemini API and AI Studio, adds product-specific Notebook and Vids routes, describes the Enterprise API as coming soon, and applies named geography exclusions to AI Studio replication.
claims.sourceLocator: S1 Start using section and AI Studio geography footnote; the article explicitly does not generalise the exclusions to every API route.

claims.text: Google says every Gemini Audio clip carries SynthID and mentions C2PA with replication safeguards, while the public evidence does not clearly document route-by-route C2PA verification coverage.
claims.sourceLocator: S1 trust and transparency section; comparison with the more detailed S2 consent and profile lifecycle documentation.

claims.text: The FTC says harmful voice cloning has no single technical solution, watermarks may be removed or distorted, and false authenticity signals can be harmful in sensitive settings.
claims.sourceLocator: S6 intervention-point overview, watermark limitations and bank or healthcare false-authenticity example; not represented as a Gemini assessment.

claims.text: Migration from the earlier preview moves turn direction into structured speech_metadata, requires a speaker on every multi-speaker turn and changes default unary output from raw PCM to WAV with a RIFF header.
Ignored direction, missing speaker mappings and manually wrapping an already wrapped WAV are integration failure modes that regression tests should cover.
claims.sourceLocator: Premises are the schema and output-format changes in S4; the failure modes and test advice are operational inferences.

claims.text: The VoiceEQ paper treats TTS naturalness, expressiveness, identity stability and reliability as largely independent evaluation dimensions.
claims.sourceLocator: S7 abstract; used as an evaluation framework, not as a result for Gemini 3.8 TTS.

claims.text: Google's standard launch-period audio-output prices are US$9 per million tokens for Flash and US$6 for Flash-Lite through 31 December 2026, rising to US$18 and US$12 from 1 January 2027.
claims.sourceLocator: S5 Standard pricing tables for both models and effective-date rows; prices were rechecked during factual review.

claims.text: At 25 audio tokens per second, the launch-period audio-output rates equal about 1.35 US cents per generated minute for Flash and 0.9 US cents for Flash-Lite, before text input and other system costs.
claims.sourceLocator: S5 audio-token footnote and rates; 1,500 tokens per minute multiplied by each per-million-token price.

claims.text: A deployment decision should bind voice authority, storage duration, credential access, revocation, audience disclosure, migration testing and the post-launch price before production use.
claims.sourceLocator: Operational synthesis from the documented consent and storage choices, provenance limits, migration changes, pricing change and independent evaluation context.
